The “special organization” and the “special-operations unit” have existed long since, and to this day they still appear the world over. In fact, whether in democratic states or in totalitarian ones, and no matter whether the country be advanced or backward, the great majority have activities of a like kind; it is only their scale, great or small, and their names that differ.

This state of things is enough to mirror the fact that the existence of the “special organization” and the “special-operations unit” has a value inherent in itself, and answers to needs of differing degree.

What is called the “special organization” is a system of command constituted for the carrying out of a specific mission; what is called the “special-operations unit” is an armed force of irregular form, formed up for the carrying out of a specific mission.

At present the designation prefixed with “special” has for the most part fallen out of use, and has commonly been replaced by “intelligence work”; yet “intelligence work” is but one item among the tasks of “special work,” and neither in the letter nor in the sense of it can it cover the whole of “special work.” Although the quarters concerned did once rack their brains to find a name at once agreeable to the ear and fitting, wherewith to sum up work of this kind, they never could find one, nor coin a new one either; and so the old usage has been kept up to the present day, which in truth does not suit.

Synopsis — Chapter 2, “Self-Starting, of One Heart and Mind.” This chapter shall set down in outline the “Pacification Corps” and its “First Brigade.” The “Pacification Corps” numbered in all six thousand officers, not counting the enlisted men among them. Besides the corps headquarters and its directly subordinate assault brigade, it had under it seven brigades and three directly subordinate companies, spread across the Northeast, North China, and Central China—some twenty provinces and the two special municipalities of Beiping and Tianjin. Thereafter the several units developed on the spot, sending out more than thirty “command rooms” and some two hundred and more “working groups,” together with a number of newly formed “assault teams.” Reckoned roughly, by this time the “Pacification Corps” had come to command officers and men to the number of several tens of thousands.

This “special-operations unit,” after eighteen months of grappling with the Communist army in place after place, truly suffered grievous losses: of the several tens of thousands it had once numbered, after being gathered in and reorganized at Ningbo in the spring and summer of the thirty-eighth year of the Republic, those who withdrew to Taiwan were a bare three thousand and more.

The Corps Commander of the “Pacification Corps” has said: “Were the work of the several brigades, the companies, and each of the command rooms, and of every one of our comrades, to be set down in good order, it could truly become a mighty book written in blood and tears; only, the great mansion has already toppled, the rivers and hills have changed their color, and a defeated general is in no place to speak of valor…” The writer, for his part, holds that—leaving aside whether the view that “the defeated speak not of valor” be right here or no—since there are indeed “blood and tears,” then the deeds of that shedding of blood and tears ought to be set on record, to do honor to the numberless who sacrificed themselves; it has in truth nothing to do with one man’s honor or disgrace.

The valiant deeds of the whole corps, alas, the writer cannot know in full; I can only write out the “First Brigade,” the part that was in my own charge. Such is the plain truth of it, and by no means out of any mind to favor my own and slight the rest; I beg the comrades of the several brigades to look on it with understanding.

The “First Pacification Brigade,” code-named Unit “0760,” had the area of work assigned it by its superiors take in the three provinces of Hebei, Chahar, and Suiyuan, the two municipalities of Beiping and Tianjin, and a corner of Rehe province besides.

The whole brigade had under it five command rooms, a good many directly subordinate sections, and one directly subordinate assault team, and it undertook besides the training of the fourth term of the “Lizhi Class,” a hundred and more of whose students were, every one, posted and enrolled into this brigade as its men. From the ninth month of the thirty-sixth year of the Republic, from an original establishment of six hundred officers, by the end of the thirty-seventh year it had expanded to a thousand and several hundred officers—and this without counting the assault-team men made up of non-commissioned officers. Over and above this, the armed bands it helped the local townships to organize were not few, and these of course cannot be reckoned in.

The whole brigade had three great merits which it falls to me in duty to put forward, and they are these: “to seek the new,” “to have drive,” and “to reach concord.” As for what it was we did, that shall be set down chapter by chapter in what follows.

The last section begins from the “command briefing” of unit heads, held at fixed times in Beiping, to which the “First Pacification Brigade” was invited, and goes on to set down the tale of two other gatherings of like kind to the “briefing”; the matter of them has scarcely been passed abroad, and so, though yesterday’s faded blooms, it is fresh still.

In the foregoing first chapter there appeared two technical terms, the one “special organization,” the other “special-operations unit”; these two terms are easily confounded, and may perhaps be run together as one. Let me first, then, take the sense of these two terms, and their bearing on the actual state of things at that time, and set them out with explanation, adding a little by way of extension and comment.

This was in itself a fairly dry question, one seldom talked of in the ordinary way, nay, one deliberately shunned and left untouched. And just for that reason it came to seem the more mysterious; and being mysterious, it the more readily led to misunderstanding. In truth one may speak of it quite openly—what harm is there in that?

In fact, the “special organization” and the “special-operations unit” exist the world over: whether in a democratic state or a totalitarian one, whether in an advanced country or a backward one, most have institutions of a like kind at work, and it is only their names, and their scale great or small, that differ. And this too is enough to mirror the fact that the existence of the “special organization” and the “special-operations unit” has a certain value of its own, and answers to needs of differing degree.

What is called the “special organization” is a command system constituted for the carrying out of a specific mission; whereas the “special-operations unit” is an armed force of irregular constitution, organized for the carrying out of a specific mission.

As to the continued use of the two words “special work,” in the “Long Preface” of my book Nameless Heroes it is said: “The term tewu, ‘special service,’ evolved out of ‘special assignment,’ ‘special task,’ and ‘special mission.’ When my country’s government first formally established an intelligence-training institution, it was called the ‘Special-Service Police Training Class,’ and thereafter there was the ‘Special Police Training Class,’ and so on.” Here I may add a further word of explanation, as follows: whether it be “special assignment,” “special task,” or “special mission,” all may be covered by the two words tewu, “special service”; but because the term tewu has, over long years, been wittingly or unwittingly misunderstood, made light of, cheapened, and blackened by people, one came, willy-nilly, to avoid the word tewu in speech and writing and to put “special” in its place. It is, when one comes to think of it, a matter that rather repays reflection.

Strange to tell, the word “special”—perhaps because it did not sit easily in use—never did come much into vogue. Meanwhile the quarters concerned racked their brains to find a name at once agreeable to the ear and fitting, wherewith to sum up work of this kind, but they never could find one, nor coin a new one either. Who it was that hit upon the notion, or whose suggestion was taken up, I do not know; but somehow, half against the grain, the word “intelligence” came to be used. Strictly speaking, “intelligence” is but one item within “special work,” and neither in the letter nor in the substance can it cover the whole of “special work”; yet, once it was used, so it has gone on being used, by mere force of habit, down to the present.

From this we may understand that “special work” is “special-service work,” which is what is now generally called at home “intelligence work.” At the time of the thirty-sixth year of the Republic, what was called the “special organization” meant the “Baomiju,” reconstituted out of the “Juntong Bureau”; the long-established “Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Central Party Headquarters” (in brief the “Zhongtong”); and certain field units under the “Second Bureau of the Ministry of National Defense.” Besides these, there were one or two small units given over solely to the gathering (and study) of international intelligence.

As for the “special-operations unit,” its distinction from the “special organization”—beyond the explanation given above, namely that the “organization” is a “command system” while the “unit” is a “regular armed force”—lies also in its basic mission and in its manner of operating, in both of which they differ. One further point, and a plainer one, is that the “special-operations unit,” as a rule, wears uniform and bears arms openly; only, when need be, it may “go about its work in plain clothes.”

To speak further of precedents that have already been: such as the “Special-Duty Corps” set up in the early days of the Jiangxi bandit-suppression in the twenty-second and twenty-third years of the Republic (be it noted that biedong, “special duty,” means just this special-duty work); the “Transport Police Corps,” reorganized after the victory in the War of Resistance out of the “Loyal and Patriotic Army” (though in name it was called the “Transport Police,” in fact it was given over solely to the putting-down of the bandit army’s rebellion); and the “Ministry of National Defense People’s Service Corps,” organized in the spring of the thirty-sixth year in Sichuan out of the Youth Army, and the present “Ministry of National Defense Pacification Corps”—all these belong to the “special-operations unit.” The “special-operations unit” is of a temporary nature, not brought into the order of battle of the “regular forces”; the moment its mission is fulfilled, or the circumstances change and its object vanishes, it is disbanded or reorganized. The “special-operations unit” must not, either, be run together with the “special-arms troops.” The “special-arms troops” are distinguished by “arm of service”—such as “engineers,” “artillery,” “paratroops,” “armor,” “chemical troops,” and the like, all of which are “special-arms troops.” The “special-operations unit,” by contrast, is set toward a special mission.

In recent years my country no longer uses terms of the sort “special-service work” or “special work,” but commonly calls them “intelligence work” instead. In the “Long Preface” of my book Nameless Heroes I once set forth the following opinion upon the use of the term “intelligence work”: “To use ‘intelligence work’ to cover intelligence, action, sabotage, subversion, counter-espionage, psychological warfare, political warfare, assault, guerrilla operations, and all the other special duties is not comprehensive; and it is very easily confounded with the professional ‘gathering of intelligence,’ ‘processing of intelligence,’ ‘employment of intelligence,’ and so on.” For all that, down to the present the term “intelligence and security units” is still in general use, and everyone knows what it means. Which is to say, the “special organization” of former years has been replaced by today’s “intelligence and security units.”

To speak again of the “special-operations unit”—at present, I suppose, it no longer exists; and if it does, then by the look of it, it can have but one mission, that of dealing with the puppet régime that has usurped the mainland.
With the foregoing notions in hand, the reader will find it the easier, in what follows, to enter into the matter.

The “Lizhi Class” trained one term every few months; at Nanjing, first and last, only three terms were held before it was stopped—and why? That, of course, had to do with the general situation turning day by day against us. The First Brigade held one term of its own in Beiping, which its superiors sanctioned as the fourth term of the “Lizhi Class,” and there was only this one. There was said to be a fifth term besides, at Changtai in Fujian, but all that is a later story.

How many students in all passed through the training of the “Lizhi Class” there ought to be some official record; and if there is, it has long since been buried in the old files, and there is now no way to look it up. At a rough reckoning, it must come to above a thousand, I should think.

Not long after the first term’s training began, there befell in the class an incident of which even many in the class knew nothing—a thing that ought not to have happened yet did, and that truly will not bear excusing. And so I had not meant, at first, to write it out, lest I lay bare my own shortcomings and even become a laughing-stock to the learned. But it is a matter to take warning from as well, and one that can, moreover, expose the deep-laid scheming of the Communist Party, and how it leaves no crack unpenetrated. And if these reasons be not enough—then what of the effect that the occurrence of incidents of this kind brings in its train? That too must be put forward for a little study.

The facts of the matter went thus. One day the Corps Commander, Mr. Liu Peichu, gathered all the students in the classroom to address them, his theme being the “four great tasks” of our corps; and he urged them besides to become masters all-round in the four—“pacification,” “intelligence,” “action,” and “assault.” At this time the Corps Commander was speaking from the platform, while the training officers, section leaders, and the rest went about below, now and again, on their rounds. In the course of his rounds the section leader Wang Zhaofen suddenly caught sight of two students who, while feigning to listen to the address, were passing a little pellet of paper back and forth between them; seeing which, Section Leader Wang hurried forward to demand: “What are you doing?”—and bade them bring out the little paper pellet they had just been passing to and fro. At this, one of the two, seeing that things looked ill, in his flurry gave the pellet a few more twists and thrust it hastily into his trouser pocket. But Section Leader Wang was quick of eye and would not let them hide it away; he searched out the pellet on the instant, and, spreading it open, saw that the two had written, one to the other, three sentences. The first ran: “This whole line he is preaching is very much against our interest”; the second: “Luckily the others have not taken it in”; the third: “Or else—are they not all listening rapt?” Of these three exchanged sentences, the first is the most suspicious: what is this “very much against our interest”? And just whom did the word “we” refer to? Thereupon the two men were led out of the classroom and closely interrogated, while those in the classroom knew nothing of what was toward. The writer himself was present at the time, yet of this affair my impression has already grown dim.

According to Wang Zhaofen—the fellow-student who was going his rounds of the classroom at the time and found the thing out (a section leader during the training, a commanding officer after the postings)—as he tells it: “Under interrogation, the two bowed their heads and owned that they were both Communists, and, brazen-faced, said threateningly: ‘If you kill us, you will surely meet with revenge one day.’” Wang Zhaofen recalls further: “One of the two was named Yang Rongyuan, a man of Hejian in Hebei; the other Wang Mingyang, a Shandong man. Yang Rongyuan had once been a junior officer under Liao Yaoxiang’s Sixth Army of the ‘India-Burma Expeditionary Force’; demobilized after the victory, he stayed on in the ranks, joined the ‘First Branch of the Press Training Class’ and was trained at Qijiang, and afterward transferred into the ‘Ministry of National Defense People’s Service Corps,’ whence, for his outstanding showing, he was picked out to be trained in the ‘Lizhi Class.’”

“The other, Wang Mingyang, was demobilized from the 205th Division of the Youth Army, likewise worked in the ‘People’s Service Corps,’ was a colleague of Yang Rongyuan’s and a fellow-conspirator besides, and, for his good showing, was picked at the same time to be trained in the ‘Lizhi Class.’” Such, in the main, was how the matter stood. As for when and where they had joined the Communist Party, at whose bidding they had infiltrated the “Lizhi Class,” what mission they bore, and what their design may have been—since the whole case had been handed over to the responsible unit to deal with, I inquired no further. And as for what “confession” the two men made, whether there was any further implication, and what came of it in the end—of that we know nothing at all.
Strange to tell—that an affair so full of excitement should leave me not one shred of memory to call back!

Of this affair there is a brief record in the Corps Commander Mr. Liu Peichu’s posthumous work Fleeting Glimpses of a Floating Life, which runs: “They were forthwith arrested and interrogated, and it proved true that they owned to being Communists; but as the training was then in progress and there was no leisure to attend to it, they were handed over to the ‘Bureau of Investigation and Statistics’ to be dealt with.” From this it would seem that the higher authorities did not, after all, press the question of responsibility for this incident.

To speak first of how they were found out: these two men were either rash or green; how could they, under the eyes of the whole assembly, write the words of their hearts on a scrap of paper and toss it back and forth? Did they never think of the consequences, once they were caught? If they wished to exchange views, opportunities there were in plenty, and time as well—why must it be on just such an occasion as this? These two little Communists, as I see it, were most likely no more than a pair of “fledglings,” drawn over and then never schooled, with no seasoning of their own to speak of.

On the other hand, if the Corps Commander Mr. Liu Peichu’s account be indeed the truth of it, then his “having no leisure to attend to it, and handing them over to the ‘Bureau of Investigation and Statistics,’” smacks much of treating the thing as no concern of his own and passing it over in a single stroke—nor is it without something open to question. Anyone can imagine what a grave matter it was that two Communists should have penetrated into our special-training institution: one cannot merely make certain that these two fellows were Communists and be done with it by pushing them out the door. To my own way of thinking, unless the Corps Commander Liu had already made some remedial disposition that he was ashamed to set down, or feared it inconvenient to expose too much, then the following procedures and points of care ought to have been carried out, to wit: first, to make at once a report, oral or written, of the whole facts to the class director Mr. Zheng Jiemin, and to seek his instruction on the principle of disposal—for the head of the “Lizhi Class” ought to be the class director, and not the Corps Commander.

Second, following the selection process, to make a thorough investigation of how these two bandits had got into the “Lizhi Class”—though responsibility need not necessarily be pressed, still one must get the whole course of the thing clear to the bottom; the more so as the Corps Commander of the moment was the very Corps Commander of the “People’s Service Corps” in which these two had worked, and so bore a responsibility not to be shrugged off.

Third, letting the rest go for the moment—before handing them over, one must, at the very least, ascertain what these persons had already done within the “Lizhi Class,” and whether there were yet other confederates.
Over and above this, if one is to speak of special training, here was a real teaching-piece for education-by-occasion—why not put it to good use?
Supposing there were scruples, one might still trim and prune it, casting out the chaff and keeping the grain, and it would lose nothing of being a first-rate lecture-piece.
What I have said above speaks to the reason of the thing; I have no mind to wrangle to the death, nor to pick faults for their own sake.
This affair I set down thus far and no further; as for what became of the two, Wang Mingyang and Yang Rongyuan, that indeed we none of us know.

To go on: after the first term of the “Lizhi Class” had graduated, the “Pacification Corps” was forthwith established; and besides the postings and assignments, the second and third terms of the “Lizhi Class” were held one hard upon another.

Having looked into a good deal of relevant material, and inquired besides of the memory of fellow-students and comrades here in Taiwan, and adding my own understanding thereto, I give the establishment and strength of the “Pacification Corps” roughly as follows. The “Pacification Corps” was seated at Nanjing (the address being the Capital Market at Sixiang Bridge on Zhuque Road), and had under it in all seven brigades, three directly subordinate companies, and one directly subordinate assault brigade.
The seven brigades were seated, in order, in Hebei, the Northeast, Shandong, Henan, Shanxi, Hubei, and Anhui.
The three directly subordinate companies were spread about the Jiangsu-Zhejiang region.

Each brigade had, on formal appointment (within the establishment), officers to the number of two hundred and more, and, as employed personnel (outside the establishment), on the pay-grade of first and second lieutenants, four hundred and more, making six hundred and more together. All that is here reckoned are “officers”; there were no enlisted men.

Reckoning the seven brigades, the three directly subordinate companies, and the corps headquarters together, there were in all more than six thousand officers. It was too vast—vast beyond all precedent.
Under each brigade were set command rooms, and under the command rooms working groups; the whole corps had more than thirty command rooms and more than two hundred working groups.

As to the organization of the “corps headquarters”: besides the Corps Commander and Deputy Corps Commander, there were the chief of staff, the political director, and the staff and administrative sections and the like. Herewith, drawing on the record in the book Recollections of the Treasure Isle by Mr. Zhang Zhendong—deputy of the Third Brigade of the “Pacification Corps” and concurrently colonel commanding officer of the “Fourth Command Room of Northern Anhui”—together with some scraps of hearsay and the writer’s own fragmentary memory, the names and brief careers of the several brigade commanders under the “Pacification Corps” are as follows: First Brigade commander, Chen Gongshu, fifth class of the Military Academy; Second Brigade commander, Chen Zhenshan, tenth class of the Military Academy; Third Brigade commander, Liu Renhua, later Wang Dexin; Fourth Brigade commander, Guo Chongxin, later Yang Zhengzhi; Fifth Brigade commander, Jin Yifu, fifth class of the Military Academy; Sixth Brigade commander, Xiang ——, particulars unknown; the Seventh Brigade, it is said, was never formed, though by one account its commander was surnamed Yu; the commander of the First Directly Subordinate Company, Guan Rongde; the rest still unknown. The above is the outline touching the “Pacification Corps”; should there be errors in it, or should new material come to light, they shall be corrected and supplemented when the fifth book is published.

Here what the writer would particularly put forward is this: the whole corps’ numbers are roughly reckoned at six thousand and more, though in fact, by reason of the several brigades’ growth, they must have far exceeded this figure; and after two years of grappling with the Communist Party, the losses may be called grievous indeed! Reorganized afterward at Ningbo, those whom the Corps Commander Liu brought over to Taiwan were only 3,500—and this body of men were not necessarily all of them the same men who had been there when the “Pacification Corps” was newly formed; which is to say, those on the mainland already fallen, missing, or taken prisoner came to above 2,500 in all, nay, to several times over that figure. And who among them were they? Save for the few whose names can still be told, all the rest became “nameless heroes”! Even as the saying has it: a hero need leave no name, and they who leave a name are not all of them heroes.

“First Brigade, Ministry of National Defense Pacification Corps” was our formal designation. The brigade had a brigade-standard, and it was just these eleven characters that were written upon it. Had a board been hung at the main gate, these same eleven characters would surely have been written on it too. Only, try as I will, I cannot recall whether we ever had a standard at all; and as for the matter of the board, let me ask about among them, and add the fact when I have it clear.

“Hebei Brigade” was the short name, rather like a man’s byname. Now and again some called it “North China Brigade” as well; but in truth neither “Hebei Brigade” nor “North China Brigade” was quite apt: for the area of work assigned by our superiors was not confined to the single province of Hebei, while for the three provinces of the North China region—Shandong, Henan, and Shanxi—there were the Third, Fourth, and Fifth Brigades besides.

Unit “0760” was the code-name conferred by the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters.” Setting aside those in plain clothes, upon the insignia worn by every officer of this unit in uniform were printed the four Arabic figures (0760). To speak of Unit “0760” was to strike a far more resounding note: throughout the Beiping-Tianjin region and the scores of counties of Hebei province it had left a very fair name, and above all in the places where the bandit army had come and gone time and again and worked its ravages, the common folk had of Unit “0760” an impression both good and deep. Nor was that all: in the bandit army’s captured documents we more than once came upon intelligence bearing on the doings of “0760.” This, at the least, proves that we had our effect, and that the Communist side kept its eyes upon us.

Writing thus far, the writer may as well disclose a bygone thing in which “vanity” played its mischief. My post was, of course, that of brigade commander; a brigade commander is naturally greater than a company commander, a sub-brigade leader, or a squad leader, and for people to address me as “brigade commander” was the most natural thing, having not the least to do with exalting or belittling. Yet whenever I heard the address “brigade commander,” I always felt something hard to put into words, and was ill at ease. It may be that this was not vanity alone, but had mixed in it some element of an “inferiority complex” as well. But if someone called me “unit commander,” I felt of a sudden a good deal greater, as though only this fitted just to the measure—when in truth brigade commander and unit commander are one and the same; and to think of it makes me laugh at myself.

Nowadays—that is, in the present, the seventy-fifth year—it is otherwise: whenever I meet an old comrade-in-arms and he hails me with a “brigade commander,” I feel it so warm and near, and it is most pleasant to the ear. Were someone now to call me “unit commander,” it would, on the contrary, be flat and savorless.

Idle talk aside, let me go on to speak in more detail of our “First Brigade.” Mr. Li Yulin had an old acquaintance with the Corps Commander Mr. Liu Peichu (Liu had been administrative inspector of the Tangshan district of Hebei province, and Li chief of the Tangshan municipal police), and it was on the Corps Commander Liu’s recommendation that Li Yulin took up the post of deputy commander of the First Brigade. Before this, Mr. Li Yulin and I were not acquainted. Though Mr. Li had been chief of staff of the “Sixth Route Army of the North China Loyal and Patriotic Army” while I was deputy commander-in-chief of the “North China Loyal and Patriotic Army,” still we had never met. Yet, being both of us men who had come through hard times together, we truly took to each other at first sight.
Before the first term of the “Lizhi Class” had graduated, the deputy commander Li had already gone on ahead, back to Beiping, to prepare for the setting-up of the brigade headquarters.

Put it thus: through the period of preparation the First Brigade headquarters rested wholly on the deputy commander Li, running to and fro alone; by the time I reached Beiping he had already found and fixed on office quarters at Xishiku (a street-name). Rude and makeshift though they were, got up on funds as scant as scant could be, it was as good as raising a tower with empty hands.
Why, not long after, we moved again from Xishiku to the rear court of Tieshizi Hutong in the eastern city, I cannot recall.

The front court of the brigade headquarters’ new site was in fact the main gate of the “Police Officers’ School”; whether this “Police Officers’ School” was a branch class of the “Central Police Officers’ School” I did not look into. Since the First Brigade headquarters lay in the rear court of the “Police Officers’ School,” and it would have been inconvenient for both parties to go in and out by the one gate, we opened a gate of our own in the rear wall and set a separate guard upon it. This, in fact, gave onto yet another street—the street called “Fuxue Hutong.”

The “Police Officers’ School” stood on the north side of the eastern mouth of Tieshizi Hutong; old as the building was, its grandeur was still no common thing—for here, as it turned out, had stood the “Provisional Executive Government” of the days when Duan Qirui held the chief executive’s power, in the thirteenth and fourteenth years of the Republic. In those days the writer was at middle school and often passed through Tieshizi Hutong, and a broken impression of it lingers with me yet. In the twenty-seventh year of the Republic, the writer, riding in a pedicab from Dongsi North Avenue to Beixinqiao, passed by the outer eastern mouth of Tieshizi Hutong, and saw only that there was a Japanese sentry standing guard at the mouth of the lane—but I did not know by what organ of the Japanese army it had been taken over. This span of recollection reaches, first and last, more than sixty years.

The part made over to our brigade headquarters was, in its main body, a two-story building, and there was besides a building serving the triple use of classroom, mess-hall, and assembly-hall—quite spacious, able to hold two or three hundred. To the right as one entered was a row of single-story houses, used for the “guard section” and the “wireless station.” The upper floor of this main building was partitioned into seven or eight rooms, serving severally as the conference room, the offices of the commander and deputy commander, the political director’s office, and the workplaces of the staff, quartermaster, and other business and administrative sections. Being long unrepaired, it had not, indeed, fallen to ruined tiles and toppling walls, but the peeling showed on every side. I remember that winter, when a coal fire was lit below-stairs for warmth, and dense smoke came curling up, wisp on wisp, through the cracks in the floorboards, every morning the same, and always a good twenty or thirty minutes before it would clear away—truly choking past all bearing.
For all that, no one cried out at the hardship, and no one complained; all of us knew that the bitter days were yet to come!

The first term’s students reached Beiping in the ninth month of the thirty-sixth year, when we were still at Xishiku. The second term’s students reached Beiping, I think, in the eleventh month, by which time we had already removed to the present site at Tieshizi Hutong. The third term’s students were not posted to the First Brigade. And afterward we were sanctioned to hold a term of our own at Beiping under the name of the “Lizhi Training Class,” numbering a hundred and more, and this was the fourth term.

All the students posted in from the “Lizhi Class” were enrolled into the “First Pacification Brigade”; those originally of higher rank and stronger ability were made commanding officers or section leaders, and the rest were all made brigade men, the lowest rank among them being second lieutenant.

Now let me explain further the “establishment” of the whole brigade. “Establishment” is a term in the “science of military organization”; the writer took this course too while at the Military Academy, and has long since forgotten it clean away. So then, roughly and carelessly—there may be errors, but they will not be wildly off—I set down the true state of it. The “First Brigade of the Pacification Corps” had once an “establishment table,” wherein were listed: “brigade commander, one, colonel”; “deputy commander, one, colonel or lieutenant-colonel”; “political director, one, lieutenant-colonel”; “brigade deputy, one to two, major or lieutenant-colonel”; and so on—“brigade commander” being the post, “one to two” the number of places allowed, and “colonel” the establishment-rank. By establishment-rank is meant the rank as set in the establishment. In that age, cases of a high rank taking a lower post—such as a colonel filling a lieutenant-colonel’s post—or a low rank holding a higher establishment—as lieutenant-colonels each filling colonels’ posts—were everywhere to be met with, and there was no strictness in it. The most important point is that, though all had rank, few had ever been formally appointed to “office”; and why? Because it was an age of disorder, and military organization had not yet got onto its tracks.

Besides the commander and deputy commander, political director, brigade deputy, staff officers, and quartermaster already mentioned above, there were the wireless-station chief, the radio operators, the cipher clerks, the guard-section leader, the guards, the orderlies, and so on. Over and above this, there was, it seems, no such title as “secretary”; and the reason it was not in the establishment yet was there in fact was to give cover to the doings of the “Beiping directly subordinate section”—that is, one of those so-called “measures of expediency” that forever overstepped the rules and yet made a plausible case for themselves.

The above is the brigade headquarters, that is, the command center. By rights there should be, at this point in the “establishment table,” a “sub-total of persons”; but I cannot clearly recall how many there were—to put it in a phrase of the “common folk,” with the guard section thrown in there must have been a hundred or so, I dare say?

To speak now of the field: under the brigade were four command rooms. First, the First Command Room, stationed at Zhuoxian, its field of work the northern section of the Ping-Han railway. Its commanding officers, first and last, were three men: Wang Zhaofen, Jiang Tian, and Liu Yuanshen.

Second, the Second Command Room, stationed at Jinghai, its field of work the northern section of the Jin-Pu railway. Its commanding officers, first and last, were two men, Liu Yuanshen and Chang Shaozeng. Third, the Third Command Room, stationed at Xugezhuang, its field of work the Bei-Ning line within Shanhaiguan. Its commanding officers, first and last, were two men, Pang Zhaofeng and Wang Zhaofen.

Fourth, the Fourth Command Room, stationed at Zhangjiakou, its field of work along the line of the Ping-Sui railway; its commanding officers, first and last, were two men, Zhang Xiaopu and Zhang Luying.

Fifth, the four command rooms above were the original establishment; afterward we were sanctioned to add a Fifth Command Room, stationed at Shunyi, its field of work the line running from Beiping by way of Gubeikou to Chengde. Its commanding officer was Zhang Zuoxing.

The “command room” was the working center of gravity of each brigade; whether the whole of the work could be unfolded rested wholly on whether the “command room” did or did not bestir itself to act—and the key to acting or not acting lay in how one adapted to the several different circumstances, and in the spirit of boring in and driving deep. To be sure, it is easy to say in a few words, but by no means simple to do.

The chief officer of the “command room,” of establishment-rank lieutenant-colonel, was styled “commanding officer” and not “commander”; whether this was the first instance of the kind in my country’s “military organization” I dare not say for certain, but for the writer himself it was the first time he had met with it, and if I am wrong, why then it is a case of wondering at the little one has seen. As for the Chinese Communist army, it has the appellation “command-and-combat men,” which stands for the “instructor” and the “combatant”—and this is a different thing from the “commanding officer.”

At the headquarters of the “command room” were set one operations staff officer and one intelligence staff officer, and several officers besides in charge of personnel, quartermastering, documents, and administration. Below them were set working groups or small groups, their number decided as the actual case required. Though by the establishment there might be three to five, in specially large districts there would be more than this number. “Working groups” and “small groups” might be set up mixed together—that is, there were large “working groups” and small “small groups.” Each “working group” ran from five or seven men to more than ten; a “small group” had but three or five men.

By the establishment, the strength of each “command room” was somewhere above one hundred and below one hundred and fifty. In the early period each command room kept within this limit; but later, as the work unfolded, it came to the pass of “growing by day and by night”! And how was that? Those coming to offer their service grew more and more, by dark and by daylight alike; and of the captured “bandit cadres,” too, there were often those who came over, saying: “If you do not kill me, I will follow you and work, and turn round and fight the Communists.” Could one refuse to take such men in? And so it was that they “grew by day and by night.” The phrase carries a touch of overstatement, but used here it is no exaggeration. Not every command room was so, indeed, but there were truly such cases. To speak again of the “assault team”: to use a body made up of officers to storm the Communist army’s militia, sentry posts, or small detachments was not only uneconomical in the use of manpower, but was, moreover, to put great talent to petty use. And so we proposed to our superiors to organize separately an “assault team” with non-commissioned officers for its backbone, directly subordinate to the brigade headquarters, and then, as the case required, to attach the whole team or a part of it to the several command rooms. This proposal being sanctioned, our First Brigade, besides its five command rooms, had one directly subordinate “assault team.”

The “assault team” was made up of some three hundred men; and because the several command rooms all had this same need, yet felt the distribution of force to fall short, they were allowed, “on the principle of strict selection and within the bounds of what the supply capacity permitted, to report for sanction and set them up on their own”—and so there came to be assault teams belonging to the command rooms as well. Besides those listed above, there were the “directly subordinate sections”; and the “directly subordinate section” fell again into two different forms: the one a working group given to the “four great tasks”—such as the “Northern Suburb Section” in the near outskirts of Beiping and the like; the other a business group given solely to the gathering of intelligence—such as the “Intelligence Section” lying hidden in Tianjin, and the like.
Of the “directly subordinate sections” there were a good several, and I shall introduce, one by one in what follows, the showing they made in their work.

Summing up the organization at all these levels, from the brigade headquarters down to the several small groups, the First Brigade had officers and men to the number of a thousand and several hundred, already exceeding the sum of the within-establishment strength and the four hundred employed personnel. (The local armed bands under this unit’s command are not yet reckoned in.) And here at once the problem arose: how could the rations and pay for six hundred supply the needs of more than a thousand? This must be told from the beginning. In our brigade headquarters there was, quite simply, no one who understood “quartermastering”; the deputy commander Li and I took counsel, and he was to go first and find out which unit had charge of supply for the Beiping-Tianjin region, and then to inquire whether there were any acquaintance within it. This was easy: Beiping, it was learned, came under the “Fifth Supply Department” of the Combined Service Forces Headquarters, whose commander was surnamed Geng; and under the “Fifth Supply Area” there was besides a “Sixth Depot Superintendency,” whose superintendent was surnamed Lü, and it was this depot that saw to the supply of the “First Pacification Brigade.” But trades are sundered as by mountains, and we had not one acquaintance there. The deputy commander Li and I took counsel again, and decided that the brigade headquarters should send out an official letter, setting forth the whole case, and ask the Depot Superintendency to introduce a quartermaster to us, that he might see to all matters of supply. Perhaps it was that this official letter was well written—for in our wording we used no such words as “introduce” or “recommend,” but asked him to “assign” one. Sure enough, quite smoothly, a quartermaster was “assigned” to us, and our supply problem was thereby, in substance, resolved.

This newly appointed quartermaster major was named Nie Enjun, a man of Hefei in Anhui, a graduate of the Quartermaster School, and at the time a major section-chief of the “Sixth Depot Superintendency.” After he came, the brigade headquarters made over to him the charge of all that touched supply; and save for the needful formalities that could not but be signed, the deputy commander and I from that time never had to trouble our heads over it—by which one may see how able and capable he was. As for by what arts he contrived to cut the long to piece out the short, and to shift and scrape together from here and there, so that the whole unit wanted for nothing in rations and pay—that I shall tell of hereafter; only, here I must first make one thing plain: he was a man upright and exact, not slack by a hair.

Besides the quartermaster we had brought in—ideal enough and up to the standard—our brigade had also a political director who had come along with the brigade and stood for a steadying force: he was the very Lieutenant-Colonel Luo Jing already introduced in the foregoing chapter. The political director Luo had charge of ideological assessment and of personnel promotions and the like; leave of absence and the borrowing of money were his to see to as well; and, of course, he was also the one who reported and enforced the upholding of military discipline. He had a gravity about him, and was, moreover, held in respect by the whole brigade.
Personnel and funds being both in trusty hands, the energy and time thus spared could be bent wholly upon important business—and this, too, became a merit of ours.

In the past, during the writer’s years of work in the “Juntong Bureau,” a station chief or a district chief had only a secretary and no deputy at all; this time there was a deputy commander—and how to work together? how to get on? It was, in truth, a test. I gave the matter very earnest thought, and concluded that, beyond treating each other with sincerity, what was needed was that each should understand the other. Only with understanding can there be mutual forbearance; with forbearance comes common ground; and with common ground, everything is easily done. And sure enough, we were not only good colleagues—the friendship between us lasted, to the very day he kept his eightieth birthday, when we still made merry over a cup of wine together!

In the brigade headquarters there were, moreover, many brigade deputies, staff officers, and the like, within the establishment and without, and not a few of them held on over-strength. And why use so many men? To speak in fairness, it was to lay up a store of cadres for the spreading-out of the work; and if I color it a little, I may as well own that it was to gather in men of talent. The above has merely drawn, from the establishment alone, an outline of the “First Brigade of the Pacification Corps”; let me go on now to put forward some few features of this “special-operations unit,” and its significance for the age. First: the young men of high purpose who joined this “special-operations unit” of ours grew more and more in number—which runs clean counter to the saying then current that “faith in anti-Communism was being shaken.” How, then, is this to be explained? The answer must be this: there were some who, in extreme discontent with the present state of things, sought a new environment in which they too had a part—that is, in which they had a “sense of participation”—and it was not that they truly believed in Communism and inclined toward the Communist Party. To put it more roundly still: the low spirits of young people in general in this period had no direct bearing on political faith.

Second: the scale of a single brigade is, to be sure, not to be called great, but their aspiration to try their powers was no small one; they were new-born calves that fear nothing; their nature was pure, without selfish desire, and so they had a surge of drive. Only with drive can there be gathered the force to break through the hard passes.

Third: a body of men, be it great or small, prizes a whole harmony; and because we dealt fairly and justly, from top to bottom we were of a whole harmony. As for being open or not open—that, given the special nature of the work, had its own fixed measure, and, all having forbearance, no such demand was pressed. Summing up all the above—“to seek the new,” “to have drive,” “to reach concord,” a pure-hearted solidarity, and hearts set upon achieving something—these became, then, our distinctive features.

I had only one set of grass-green everyday army uniform, of herringbone cloth and faded, issued by the “Lizhi Class”; worn all crumpled and creased on the body, it was not the least bit trim, and there could be no speaking at all of the martial bearing a soldier ought to have. What is more, to wear the uniform without the accoutrements properly in order was to look like a straggler, and on the road the gendarmes would interfere; yet with the accoutrements on, one’s movements were greatly hampered. On foot or by tram it might pass; but to sit in a pedicab and go parading through the streets was too unseemly by far.
To put it plainly, I simply did not like wearing the uniform; but, being appointed to a military post, not to wear it would not do either.

At this time, in the ninth and tenth months, the climate of Beiping was not merely cool but had a chill in it, and I really ought to have added a garment; but my pay was a paltry thing, money was wanted at every turn, and for the moment I could not see to it. In my helplessness, all at once I bethought me of the “Ying Yuantai Tailor Shop”—better go first and have a suit made, and settle the account by and by.

Speaking of the “Ying Yuantai Tailor Shop,” I cannot but call to mind a bygone thing, and this old tale I shall not forget my life long. The proprietor of the “Ying Yuantai Tailor Shop” was old Mr. Ying Yuanxun, and the tie between us was, over and above that of shopkeeper and customer, one of friendship as well. In the fourth month of the twenty-second year of the Republic, that time when we (the “Beiping Station” and the “Tianjin Station”) were ordered to sanction the traitor Zhang Jingyao, we spied several days within the Hôtel des Wagons-Lits in the Legation Quarter, and simply could not find out on which floor, in which room, Zhang Jingyao was lodging. By good luck, all unmeaning, at the turn of the stairs I ran into the proprietor Ying, and, exchanging a word of greeting, learned that he had come to deliver clothes to and fit a pattern for Military Governor Zhang (Jingyao)—and so, by the oddest chance, hit the mark in my inquiry (for the full account see the first part of my book Nameless Heroes, “Rooting Out Traitors in the North”). This was already a thing of more than ten years ago. In the second year of the War of Resistance, when the writer went from Tianjin to Beiping over the Wang Kemin case, I passed once again before the door of this tailor shop; but it was just after the action had been taken, and, fearing to bring trouble upon him, I dared not go in. This time, even had I no thought of having clothes made, I ought still to have gone to the door to see my old friend.

The shop was the same old shop, a single frontage, rustic and homely, not the least bit striking to the eye. As I stepped in, there was no one at the counter; only when I had called out, “Shopkeeper Ying! Brother Ying!” did someone come out from the back; and he, seeing that it was I, came round from behind the counter in two or three quick strides, took me by the hand, and said over and over, “Are you well? are you well!” The meeting of old friends made it doubly near and dear, and of our talk over all that had parted us there is no need to tell. When I had made plain my errand, he was for making two suits: one an army uniform, in the most fashionable gray-green “Roosevelt serge,” and another a Zhongshan tunic, in navy-blue serge, to come back a day later to try the pattern, and in five or six days they would be rushed out. I thought this good too: an army uniform kept by but not used; and for going about outside hereafter, better to wear the Zhongshan tunic—was that not a deal handier? And so it was settled. As for money, what we owed him running up was no small sum, yet the proprietor Ying never haggled or weighed it out. He said besides: “In a few days, when I have gotten up a party, we must have a good gathering; there is a ‘Han Family Cooking’ that is very fine—I shall stand treat.” The mention of “Han Family Cooking,” or “Tan Family Cooking,” is likewise reckoned a small anecdote of Beiping in the nineteen-forties, and the writer, having a mind to it, sets down what he knows: at that time there were, it seems, two such family eating-houses in all, the one surnamed Han, and so called “Han Family Cooking,” the other surnamed Tan, and so called “Tan Family Cooking,” the case of the two being much alike; and which of them, after all, it was that we ate at, I truly cannot clearly recall. But to speak of this one: what set it apart in form from an ordinary eating-house was that it had no shop-name, no signboard—thoroughly made a family affair. Only one table a day was allowed, and one had to book several days ahead, commonly waiting three to five days before one’s turn came round; the board was laid out in this family’s parlor, its setting quiet and elegant, without the least dust and din, so that, even before one had sat down to table, one already felt very much at ease.

It was said that the master of this house had originally been a civil servant, most likely the descendant of some minor capital official who had settled in Beiping in years gone by. In ordinary days he must have been most particular about his food and given to no productive labor; and in his later years, eating into a hollow hill, he bethought him of earning a few coppers on “eating,” to eke out his outlay—yet could not shake off the deep-rooted notions of the scholar-gentry, and so hit upon certain strange devices to keep his countenance. In truth it was no more, at most, than a comforting of himself.

Whenever the feast was set, a seat was first left empty to await the master; and though the cup and chopsticks were laid out for him all the same, yet unless the guests were familiars or persons of high and refined character, the master would not only not take his seat, but would not even come out to give a word of greeting.

I heard, too, that in this house the master directed the dishes from behind the scenes, while the mistress did the buying and headed the kitchen; and as for the one who tended the table, she was a middle-aged woman—though from her dress and bearing it was hard indeed to make out her standing; some said she was a servant of many years, and others that she was the concubine who held the place of “Number Two.”

As for the menu, it was all of genuine stuff and true, changing with the season; and though the number of dishes was not great, every one of them had its name and note, and their manner of cooking was in each unlike the common run. To speak of the taste—near though it came to that of Jiangsu and Zhejiang, one might rather say it gathered into one the whole achievement of the local cookery of the land, casting out its faults and taking its merits; and this is why it was called “Tan Family Cooking” or “Han Family Cooking.” If one set aside the talk of luxury and extravagance, what harm was there in regarding a fastidious care for eating as an art of living?

Someone might, perhaps, raise the question: since the trade was more than they could keep pace with, why serve only one table a day? The proprietor Ying gave the answer: “It is not for want of equipment; be the range never so large, the pot never so great, whether one fries or sautés, boils or deep-fries, one can cook only so many dishes—and if one were greedy for more, all the flavor would be lost, and it would turn into common cauldron-fare.” In the several decades since, having passed through no few places, this was the most delicious meal of all. (The writer’s note: Mr. Tang Lusun too has written of “Tan Family Cooking”; the one I ate at may perhaps not be this same house.) Some days later I fetched the newly made clothes, put the army uniform away for the while, and thereupon changed to the Zhongshan tunic. This one move truly won me no little convenience. Now, not long after I had returned to Beiping, I was invited to take part in the “weekly briefing” held at fixed times by the several local “intelligence and public-security” units (note: at the time there was as yet no such appellation as “intelligence and security unit,” and even where it now and then occurred it was not general; I use it here ahead of its time for ease of understanding). Ten and more units attended or sat in, some twenty and more persons in all. Save for a few—one or two—almost all of them were acquaintances. What made me most ashamed was that these friends had each and all come to stand on their own, their attainments beyond the common, which showed the more plainly what a good-for-nothing I was.
At every gathering all were dressed neat and trim; sorted by cut of dress, army uniforms and police uniforms were the most, with Zhongshan tunics and Western suits next.
One time it fell just on the National Day, and unlooked-for, I caught sight of a certain thing upon them—and this, again, stung me to the quick!

It turned out that some of them had pinned upon their uniforms a row or two of many-colored “ribbon bars,” among which was a length of the “Victory Medal,” given in honor of merit in the War of Resistance; I saw it with my eyes, and bitterness rose in my heart—and why? Because they had it and I had not.

Thinking of the War of Resistance, I had indeed put out my strength; only, when the thing came to the very pinch, I could not bring myself to die—so that not only did I fail to get what I ought to have gotten, but I came off with a lifelong dishonor. How could this let me hold my head up before all my brethren? A commemorative medal the less was in itself a small thing, of no account; but a scar branded into the flesh can never be dug out. And so, for a good long while, I could not but carry within me the “half-a-head-shorter” inferiority feeling; and it was this inferiority feeling, working its mischief, that made me have little to do with the outside world—unless it could not be helped, I grew cold even toward old friends of former days. Yet whether this worked any ill effect upon my work and duty is, after all, not certain.

Let me here, in passing, set down a small matter touching the “briefing.” My taking part in the local briefing—how is it to be called being “invited”? Because it was neither an order from above nor a formal notice, but merely a single summons from the head of the unit that presided over the briefing. The one that presided over the briefing was a secret unit, holding a leading place in those parts; and though this was no established system, it seemed to have become the usage.

The unit I represented—the “Pacification Brigade”—had its working center of gravity not in Beiping; and as for the “directly subordinate section” that the “Baomiju” had set me to run, it was a small unit that seemed hardly to have the standing to take part in a briefing at all. That I could now take part in the local briefing—herein was friendship, and the sense, too, of a favor shown; and in my state of mind, filled with a feeling of inferiority, I naturally felt myself already much respected, and this was true encouragement indeed.

At the briefing I was chosen by common consent to give, once a week, an “analysis of the international situation” and a “report on the bandit situation”; this, of course, I was glad to take on, but having let such things lie fallow so long, I had to put in a deal more labor at the preparing of it.

The “briefing” was like a “round-table talk,” and that all could keep up a constant connection was, on the whole, a good thing. Its use was that, in an unfixed form, one could not only exchange intelligence and exchange understandings, but could also clear away some few needless frictions, and avoid a certain amount of duplication, in the hope of taking one and the same pace and strengthening the force of the blows dealt to the enemy—and this must be called wholly to the good.

The briefing was held at a fixed time each week, and never fell behind its date; and the heads of the several units taking part attended punctually too—which was a good sign. Only, the flaw in the fine thing was that at every meeting a dozen and more motorcars were always parked outside the main gate, which not only got in the way of traffic, but the din of the drivers disturbed the peace of the neighbors as well. In that age, cars in a throng seemed the more a little showy. True, some did suggest a betterment, that it might not draw public censure; but how could it be helped, when the heads taking part in the briefing, hurrying to and fro, were all pressed for time and could not but ride in cars? And so a small matter of this sort was let slide.
Do not take this for a trifling detail—piled up, it too can lose men’s hearts!

To speak again of this briefing—held on and on, it fell away into mere form. For instance: the “work reports” put forward by the several units were, for the most part, magnifying the doings of their own quarter, or else picking out only the pleasant-sounding to tell; some, the more they said, strayed the further from the point, nay, talked past all sense. And of these, the greatest fault lay just in this, that to the hearer there was always the feeling of words not from the heart. At the meetings, too, common problems were seldom put forward for discussion, for each unit had its own several business, and their one common point was but this: how to deal with the daily more rampant “leftist” activity—which was in fact the subversive plot induced by the Communist Party. And here it may be asked: the most basic problem being left undiscussed, and no counter-measures sought—what was that for? To answer this question would take much telling; in brief, the discussing of matters of this class was not within this briefing, but belonged to a higher level, at which those taking part were not so many. Next, and without grudging the words, I set down another not-too-good feature of the briefing: in the latter half of the briefing, now and again a “constructive” criticism would be put forward, whereupon the unit concerned would be sure to make a “defensive” rejoinder in its own justification; and, to and fro, the “constructive” labored in vain, the “defensive” barred its doors fast, and the upshot not only did no good but, on the contrary, hurt the general goodwill. And here again there comes to be involved the matter of “democratic bearing” and “personal dignity”: consider—“democratic bearing” and “personal dignity” are both fairly abstract, having in themselves no measure, and how are they to be weighed? So there too there must be mixed in a certain amount of the subjective.

To be sure, that all should sit down and hold a briefing, to pool their wits for the common good and whet one another on, ought to be a good thing; only, units of this kind, set in that age, seemed still at the first learning stage as regards the democratic form, and to have reached even that pitch of the time was already very fair, and did indeed, in fact, have its effect. If one probes a step further, there is stirred up a whole train of questions—the “making public of secret work,” “whether the secret ought to lead the open,” “whether collective leadership is fitting,” and the like. Here I shall not talk of these matters, so hard to bring to a conclusion and so apt to give one a headache, but had rather tell two stories bearing upon them, by way of a partial answer.
The anti-Japanese activity in the fallen zones during the War of Resistance was, of course, all carried on in secret fashion; at the least carelessness there was the danger of some mishap befalling.

Because the “rate of mishap” was high, the workers themselves dared not lay bare their identities, nor did the higher authorities permit any lateral ties to arise—still less could there be any question of many gathering to meet together. Yet in the summer of the twenty-seventh year of the Republic, the several working units lying hidden in Tianjin—including certain “public-utility” concerns among them—leaning on the cover of the British and French Concessions, did, against all wont, have for a time a spell of “joint operations.” The units taking part were: Brother Shen Zechen, head of the “Zhongtong” in Tianjin; a certain gentleman, head of the North China branch of the “Renaissance Society”; Mr. Zhang Ziqi, director of the Tianjin Telephone Bureau; Mr. Wang Ruoxi, director of the Tianjin Telegraph Bureau; and one further, a Party worker posted to Tianjin by the Center, who now holds a fairly high place and is unwilling to have his name disclosed. And then the writer himself, taking part as chief of the “Tianjin Station of the Juntong Bureau.”

The name of this joint gathering was, I think, the “Tianjin Joint Party-Government-Military Office”—perhaps not quite right, but I can no longer recall it. What is most to be cherished in this bout of “joint operations” lay not in what it achieved, but in that spirit wherein “sincere cooperation” was sublimated into “unconditional cooperation,” and which had truly reached the pitch of self-forgetting. This was one real and solid instance, in the writer’s whole life, of each putting out his utmost, and, at the same time, a pioneering act that broke through the bounds of faction.

How the higher heads of the other units reacted to this cooperation I do not know; but afterward I was verbally reproved by Mr. Dai. For to do thus was already to have broken “the discipline of the body.”

This aside, what is worth putting forward is rather this: what force, after all, brought all to cooperate? The right answer must be—national consciousness, plus the idea of the state, multiplied again by a breast full of the heart that hates the foe and shares the common enmity!

Over and above this, it can make plain one thing further: that only the personages of the middling sort, great and small, meant to set up factions of their own, while the actual workers at the base level did not, every one of them, draw such lines of division.

At every gathering of the “joint operations,” the one presiding had beforehand made careful arrangements, to safeguard the safety of all. The matter deliberated wholly transcended the parochial spirit, and was bent upon how to withstand and to strike the common enemy—the Japanese invader. As for that friendly and warm feeling which showed itself at the gatherings, it was enough to make everyone taking part feel glad at heart. And more important still was the pure-hearted solidarity it mirrored, nay, the force born of that solidarity.

To my regret, the “joint operations” went on only about a year; for the larger circumstances changed, the Japanese invader’s devil-claws reached little by little into the British and French Concessions, a footing there grew daily harder to keep, and the several principal heads above all departed one after another, so that this makeshift combination dispersed of itself, imperceptibly. By that time the writer had already left Tianjin in the first month of the twenty-eighth year, and was transferred to Shanghai in the eighth; the particulars I have no way of knowing, and this story, too, can only stop here.

Surveying together the “joint operations” in the fallen city of Tianjin during the War of Resistance, and the “command briefing” in the city of Beiping not long after the victory, the two had their likenesses and their unlikenesses; and were one to analyze and compare them, it would not be hard to find wherein the greatest difference between them lay. To sort it out in fine could not be made clear in a few words; the writer here puts forward first two points among them. First: a war stretching over eight long years had but just ended, and the general feeling was a wish for a chance to catch one’s breath. The whole larger environment had changed, and there was yet an adapting to be done.

Second: toward the Communist Party, one part of men still remained at the stage of not seeing clearly, while another part made light of it, nay, disregarded it—and so, as to the prospects of the suppression of rebellion, they were full of optimism.

Last of all, there is yet a story of recent years—which, by the reckoning marked in the local second-hand market, ought to count as “medieval,” that is to say, neither quite new nor quite old. Still, it will be some thirty years now.

That year, in the base of revival, the writer, in the capacity of an attendant, sat in for a short time upon a high-level briefing. Though called a “briefing,” it was in fact unlike the ordinary run of briefings: to say nothing else, the moment one entered the conference room the air of it was different—grave, and hushed to a stillness where not a crow or sparrow was heard; and that whole business of greetings and handshakes and civilities was quite dispensed with. There was a feeling hard to put into words, that here everything that happened was real.
This briefing had, indeed, many an uncommon point about it—call them its distinctive features.
First: before the meeting there was full preparation in every case.
Second: in reporting, none dared tell a lie.
Third: in discussion, none dared be partial.
Fourth: once there was a decision or a conclusion reached, it had at once to be carried out.
Though scenes did arise of hard argument on the strength of reason, the reasons held to were, of course, allowed to be “straight” and not allowed to be “crooked.”

There arose, too, problems hard to decide, some of which were held over for the while, and some set for further deliberation at a fixed time; and the whole process of business was still carried on holding to the democratic principle. The writer holds that in a briefing of this kind the one presiding must have authority—and if he can be held in respect besides, so much the better. The writer has reflected, too, that this condition holds good for any line of work whatever, and is by no means confined to the military and political.
The three gatherings of differing form set out above have now been severally set down in three stories, and here they end.
